newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Students eschew politics but demand change.
newsitem.headline: Students eschew politics but demand change.

text.p: Belgrade's army of student protestors sees no irony in shunning party politics while demanding sweeping government changes and mounting massive daily marches through the streets of the capital.

Fifty years of one-party rule by communists and communists turned socialists have discredited politics to such an extent here that students seem ashamed to define their activism or themselves in political terms.
"I'm not a political person and I'm hoping not to become one," said 20-year-old Nemanja Brkovic, a journalism student, as he marched through Belgrade on Monday.
"This is not about politics and parties, it's about human rights and democracy. We had an election and the results were stolen. We were robbed. And we are responding to that theft."

Ever since Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and his ruling SPS party overturned November 17 municipal election results which went against them, the streets of Belgrade have been swarming with protestors.

The opposition political coalition Zajedno (Together) has marched for 36 straight days, drawing crowds in the tens of thousands, and sometimes in the hundreds of thousands, from Serbia's discontented middle class.
For the past 32 days Belgrade students have also marched in their tens of thousands -- always separately.
"We march separately because we're not picking sides and because we don't want to be political," explained student spokesperson Mira Milosevic -- no relation to the President.
"We don't support Zajedno but we don't oppose them either. We happen to have similar goals and demands."

Chief among those common demands is the restoration of opposition victories in a series of cities and towns, including Belgrade, where the November 17 results were overturned by SPS-controlled election commissions.
But conversations with students reveal a desire for changes far beyond the recognition of a few election results.
"You could say that having your television censored by the government is about politics but I think this is about life, about the right to live freely," explained 20-year old Dubzavka Markovic.
"Everywhere we are blockaded by the government. We have had enough of it and we are changing it ourselves, by marching, not by joining a political party."

So far neither the students nor Zajedno can point to much in the way of concrete results for their efforts, but international pressure is building behind their demand that the November 17 election results be honoured.
Those who march in the daily Zajedno processions in Belgrade are defintiely older and perhaps wiser -- most of them middle-aged and with families.
But most applaud the students and their distaste for party politics and bill themselves as protestors of last resort as well.
"I don't give a damn about politics but I do want to get rid of Slobodan Milosevic, the last communist dictator in Europe," said 34 year-old Zoran Tomic as he marched on Monday.

"The students may not know much but they know that so long as Milosevic remains in power their future is not bright. What this country needs is an orthodox economy not an orthodox communist dictator."
